nameStory: The Lettered Habrosyne gets its name from the distinctive squiggly markings across its forewings that look remarkably like cursive handwriting or ancient script. These wavy, letter-like lines give this moth the appearance of carrying a mysterious message written in an unknown language. The genus name 'Habrosyne' comes from Greek words meaning 'delicate' and 'together,' referring to the moth's graceful appearance.
description: The Lettered Habrosyne is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1.2 to 1.5 inches across. Its most striking feature is the series of dark, wavy lines that zigzag across its brown and tan forewings, creating patterns that genuinely resemble handwritten script or ancient lettering. The moth has a subtle, muted color palette of browns, tans, and grays that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. Like other members of the hooktip moth family, it has a somewhat triangular wing shape when at rest.

idTips.label: Script-like wing markings
idTips.description: Look for dark, wavy lines that zigzag across the brown forewings in patterns that truly resemble cursive handwriting or old manuscript text - this is unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Wing color and texture
idTips.description: Wings have a soft, velvety appearance in muted browns and tans with subtle gray highlights that feel almost powdery to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wingspan slightly larger than a quarter, wings appear proportionally broad compared to the body length

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a triangular tent-like shape against tree bark, where the script markings help it disappear completely

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat erratic, bouncing pattern rather than the straight-line flight of many other moths

habitat: Look for Lettered Habrosynes in mixed woodlands and forest edges where wild raspberries and blackberries grow abundantly. They're particularly common in areas with black raspberry and purple-flowering raspberry plants, as these are the only food sources for their caterpillars. You'll find them from lowland forests up into mountain areas throughout New England, especially in partially shaded areas where berry canes thrive along woodland borders.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, when you might spot them resting on tree bark during the day or attracted to porch lights at night.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August with two generations - look for fresh adults in early summer and again in late July/August. This is the best time to find them.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults may linger into early fall, but activity drops significantly after August as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Not active - overwinters in the pupal stage hidden in leaf litter or soil near raspberry patches.

funFact: The caterpillars of this 'lettered' moth are accomplished leaf architects - they actually fold and roll raspberry leaves into perfect little green sleeping bags, then live inside their custom-made leaf tents while munching their way through the walls of their edible homes.
confusionNotes: The script-like markings are so distinctive that this moth is rarely confused with other species once you know what to look for. However, when wings are folded or damaged, it might be mistaken for other brown woodland moths - but no other New England moth has those unmistakable 'handwritten' zigzag lines.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hooktip' family member, the Lettered Habrosyne doesn't actually have the pronounced hooked wingtips that give the family its name - it's more about the shared ancestry than appearance. The name 'scribe' is sometimes used interchangeably with 'lettered' for this species, both referring to those writing-like markings.
compareHints: Since this is the only Habrosyne species in New England, compare it with other Drepanidae family members like the true hooktip moths. Unlike those species with their distinctly hooked wing tips, the Lettered Habrosyne has more rounded wing tips and those unique script-like markings that no other family member displays. The combination of medium size and 'handwritten' wing patterns makes it unmistakable among New England's hooktip and false owlet moths.
